In an American paper I find this anecdote: "An old lady was being shown the spot on which a hero fell. 'I don't wonder,' she replied. 'It's so slippery I nearly fell there myself.'"

Now that story, which is very old in England, and is familiar here to most adult persons, is usually told of Nelson and the Victory . Indeed it is such a commonplace with facetious visitors to that vessel that the wiser of the guides are at pains to get in with it first. But in America it may be fresh and beginning a new lease of life; it will probably go on forever in all English-speaking countries, on each occasion of its recrudescence finding a few people to whom it is new.

It is a problem why we tend to be so resentful when an editor or a comedian offers us a jest that has done service before. It is, I suppose, in part at any rate, because we have paid our money, either for the paper or the seat, and we experience the sense of having been defrauded. We have been done, we feel, because the bargain, as we understood it, was that we were purchasing novelty. So that when suddenly an old, old jape, which perhaps we have ourselves related—and that of course is an aggravation of the grievance—confronts us, we are indignant. But what, one wonders, would a comic paper or a revue that had nothing old in it be like. We can never know.

message.content:
In an American publication, I encountered this amusing story: "An old lady was being shown the spot on which a hero fell. 'I don't wonder,' she replied. 'It's so slippery I nearly fell there myself.'" 

This tale, which has long circulated in England and is recognized by most adults, is commonly associated with Nelson and the Victory. Its frequent retelling by witty visitors to the ship has led some of the more discerning guides to preemptively share it. However, in the United States, this anecdote might still feel novel, perhaps beginning a fresh chapter in its life. It is likely to endure across all English-speaking nations, with each resurgence finding a handful of individuals encountering it for the first time.

One might ponder why we often react with irritation when an editor or a comedian presents us with a joke that has been previously shared. Part of this resentment stems from the fact that we have invested our money, whether for the publication or a ticket, resulting in a feeling of being cheated. We feel misled, as we anticipated receiving something original. Thus, when we are faced with an age-old joke, especially one we may have told ourselves—adding to our annoyance—we become quite displeased. Yet, one cannot help but speculate what a comedic magazine or performance devoid of any familiar material would resemble. That remains a mystery we will never uncover.
